card.hook: Most people crowd the university's front steps, but the best view of this palace-looking building is from across the river, where it peeks over the rooftops like it's got a front-row seat.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Lindenhof hilltop, where the University of Zurich main building is about 500 m to the south-east. Face north-east across the Limmat, and check the direction on the map before you set up.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to catch the whole scene of rooftops, church and university. Then try 2x, or up to 5x on some phones, to pick out the tower and facade. Save 0.5x for when you want lots of foreground and sky, because it makes the university look small and far away.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the tower on one vertical line, and tap the building so the facade stays clear if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Check the light on the day, because the view depends on the weather and the season.
card.selfie_here: Try the Polyterrasse, the viewing terrace beside the UZH main building, which you reach by the Polybahn funicular from near Central station. Use the front camera at 0.5x and stand with the city view behind you, but check your screen, as nothing confirms the university will show up over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pavement in front of the main entrance at Rämistrasse 71, facing the building, while you pose with the entrance behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The forecourt at Rämistrasse 71 is an entrance area, so check for event or construction closures, and check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
card.challenge: Get the tower on a gridline with the Predigerkirche right below it, and see if you can do it in three frames or fewer.
card.good_to_know: The University of Zurich, known as UZH, was founded in 1833 and was the first university in Europe set up by a state rather than by a monarch or the church. The main building at Rämistrasse 71 dates from 1914 and was designed by Karl Moser. With around 28,700 students, it's the largest university in Switzerland.

card.hook: A tram slides across the bridge, and behind it sits a huge stone arch that looks more like a palace gate than a railway station. That's Zürich HB, and the bridge opposite is the best place to see it.
card.stand_here: Head for Bahnhofbrücke, the bridge over the Limmat directly opposite the station, and stand on the upstream side. Face back toward the station so the front and the riverbank sit together in your frame. The Navigate buttons will get you there.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the station front, the riverbank and a passing tram into one picture. Then try 1x for a calmer, less stretched look at the arch, and 2x or more (if your phone has it) for the details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them, so the arch stands up straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is worth a try for softer light. Check which way the light falls on the stone front when you arrive.
card.selfie_here: Try Bahnhofplatz, on the square just outside the main arch next to the Alfred Escher monument. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a little low, so the arched entrance fills the background over your shoulder. Parked or passing cars can sit between you and the building, so you may need to wait for a gap.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Bahnhofplatz facing the main façade, while you stand in front of the Escher monument and the fountain.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge is busy, so take your time and stay clear of the tram lines and the pavement edge. Check the official site for any works or restrictions, especially before photographing inside the station.
card.challenge: Catch a tram crossing the bridge with the arch right behind it. Try a Live Photo, then pick your best frame afterwards.
card.good_to_know: Zürich HB is the largest railway station in Switzerland and one of the busiest in Europe. The sandstone neo-Renaissance building opened in 1871, designed by Jakob Friedrich Wanner. The first station on this spot opened in 1847 for the line to Baden.

card.hook: One of the world's most expensive shopping streets started life as a ditch called the Fröschengraben, the 'Ditch of the Frogs'. Today you're here for something free: a long, straight line of facades with trams gliding down the middle.
card.stand_here: Stand in Bürkliplatz, at the lake end of Bahnhofstrasse beside the tram stop and lakeside, and face north. You'll look straight back up the street towards the main station.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the classic view up the street. Try 0.5x to fit in more of the lake square and sky, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to squeeze the distant facades and trams closer together.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line up the tram tracks or the row of facades with one of the vertical lines, so the street runs straight into your picture.
card.best_time: Daytime gives you clear views along the street, but it's busy during shopping hours. A weekday evening after 18:00 is when the crowds thin out, and in December the Lucy light installation makes after-dark photos look completely different.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Paradeplatz tram island and stand with the street stretching back behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the street over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand near the bronze Alfred Escher statue at the station end and ask a passer-by to take your photo, so the street runs off behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Trams share the street, so stay on the pavement or a tram island and keep off the rails.
card.challenge: Wait for a tram to glide into your shot and see if you can catch it right on a gridline, then do a victory wave when you nail it.
card.good_to_know: Bahnhofstrasse runs about 1.4 km from the station square down to the lake. It only dates from 1864, when the old city walls were pulled down and the frog ditch in front of them was filled in. Halfway down is Paradeplatz, home to two big Swiss banks and the Confiserie Sprüngli chocolate shop and cafe.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Bürkliplatz, at the lake end of Bahnhofstrasse beside the tram stop and lakeside, and face north. You'll look straight back up the street towards the main station.

card.hook: Rodin's Gates of Hell are parked on a city square, with a sloping mirrored museum wing rising right behind them. Trams and people drift past, so every shot comes out a little different.
card.stand_here: Stand on Heimplatz in front of the Kunsthaus main entrance, facing the new mirrored wing. Rodin's Gates of Hell should sit in front of it, with the square's street life all around.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to fit the sculpture, the new wing and the square into one frame. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for details of the sculpture or the facade.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the facade, then slide the picture a little darker so the bright reflections and sky don't wash out the building.
card.best_time: Soft, even daylight, like a bright overcast day, usually suits a reflective facade best. Quieter times of day make it easier to get a clear view of the sculpture, and a little patience pays off while you wait for a tram to pass.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the bronze Gates of Hell, to the right of the main entrance on Heimplatz. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the building rise over your shoulder. If you're heading inside, the main staircase in the new building is also a good selfie spot, because its lines and light make selfies look professional.
card.ask_someone: Stand in the middle of Heimplatz beside the Ignaz-Heim-Denkmal and ask a passer-by to shoot back toward you, so the old Moser building fills the background (check it on the ground, as it's our best guess).
card.rules_and_safety: Keep to the pavement and clear of the tram tracks, especially on Rämistrasse. Check for building works or barriers on the square, as they can block the view. Inside, photos are fine without flash, selfie sticks aren't allowed, and works marked with a photography ban are off limits.
card.challenge: Get the Gates of Hell sharp in the foreground with a tram sliding past behind them, and keep your feet on the pavement while you wait for it.
card.good_to_know: The Kunsthaus is Switzerland's biggest art museum by area, with a collection running from the Middle Ages to contemporary art and a focus on Swiss artists. The original building by Karl Moser and Robert Curjel opened in 1910. David Chipperfield's big new wing began operating in October 2021 across the street, and a passage underneath links the two.

card.hook: Here's a little secret about Münsterbrücke: most people on it point their phones at the Fraumünster. Turn around and you get Zurich's famous twin towers instead.
card.stand_here: Stand on Münsterbrücke, the bridge that crosses the Limmat right next to the church. Turn around so you face the Grossmünster, which lies to the east. You'll see both towers rising over the river, with the bridge in the foreground.
card.zoom: Start at 1x, which fits the towers, river and bridge in one shot. Want more water and sky? Try 0.5x, but keep the towers away from the edges so they don't stretch. If your phone has 2x, it gives a tighter shot of the towers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the towers on one vertical line and let the river fill the bottom third of the picture.
card.best_time: Blue hour is the winner, when the church is lit up. Try night mode then, and brace your elbows on the bridge railing to keep the shot steady.
card.selfie_here: Stand right in front of the Grossmünster, at the church front, where you can see the river behind it. Or go back to Münsterbrücke and use the front camera, with the church over your shoulder. If your front camera has a 0.5x button, use it to fit more in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand along Wühre on the west bank of the Limmat and shoot across the river, while you stand on the Limmat side with the whole church behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is a place of worship, so access may be limited. Scaffolding and interior renovation have been reported on earlier visits, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get both towers in the frame with their pointy tops uncut, and the river filling the bottom. Bonus points if nobody's head pokes in.
card.good_to_know: Building began around 1100, and the church was inaugurated around 1220. The towers went up between 1487 and 1492. Their wooden steeples burnt down in 1763, and the neo-Gothic tops you see now were finished in 1787. Huldrych Zwingli started the Swiss-German Reformation here in 1520.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Münsterbrücke, the bridge that crosses the Limmat right next to the church. Turn around so you face the Grossmünster, which lies to the east. You'll see both towers rising over the river, with the bridge in the foreground.

card.hook: On a sunny day the Lindenhof wall is lined with people all pointing their phones the same way, and they've got the right idea. This is the postcard view of Zurich, and you get it from a car-free hilltop.
card.stand_here: Stand at the eastern edge of the Lindenhof, along the old wall and balustrade. Face across the Limmat to the Old Town waterfront, where the Grossmünster's twin towers sit on the far bank.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the whole river frontage and the sky. Go to 1x for a natural view of the Old Town, then zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the twin towers.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the towers, then make the shot a little darker if the sky looks washed out, and rest your elbows on the balustrade to keep zoomed shots steady.
card.best_time: Come early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the Old Town facades look warmer. Early also means fewer people along the wall.
card.selfie_here: Head down to the Schipfe, the lane at the foot of the hill, where the Lindenhof's river-side retaining wall rises above you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the hill and wall fill the space over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Limmatquai quay across the water while you stand in the Schipfe, so the hill and its retaining wall fill the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The Lindenhof is an open public park and square, and no closures or restrictions are known, but check the official site before you go. One local guide says the Grossmünster may have renovation scaffolding, so the towers might not look their best.
card.challenge: Get both Grossmünster towers on a third of the frame, with the river level and not a single elbow in the shot.
card.good_to_know: Lindenhof means 'Tilia Courtyard'. A Roman castle once stood here, followed by a Carolingian royal residence. In 1747 a second-century Roman tombstone found here gave us the oldest known mention of Turicum, the Roman name for Zurich, and in 1798 the citizens of Zurich swore their oath to the Helvetic Republic's constitution on this spot.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the eastern edge of the Lindenhof, along the old wall and balustrade. Face across the Limmat to the Old Town waterfront, where the Grossmünster's twin towers sit on the far bank.

card.hook: Picture a fairy-tale chateau parked next to Zurich's main railway station, with towers poking out above the trees. You'd half expect a drawbridge, but it's a museum, and it's very good at photos.
card.stand_here: Head into Platzspitz park and stand on the park lawns or along the Platzpromenade. Face the museum across the water. If you're coming from Zürich HB, the museum lies to the south-east, about 2 minutes on foot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole castle and the trees in one frame. Then try zoom 2x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the towers. Use zoom 0.5x only if you walk closer and want a tower's full height.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the castle, then drag the brighter/darker slider down a little so the sky stays pale instead of turning white.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is worth a try for softer light on the stonework and the water. Whatever time you come, take a few shots from different spots along the path, because small steps left or right change how the towers line up behind the trees.
card.selfie_here: Go into the museum's own courtyard, switch to the front camera and put the castle-style building behind you. Prefer the park? Try Platzspitz behind the museum, near the water feature and bandstand, with the towers over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The museum asks you not to take photos in exhibitions or of objects with a 'no-photo' sign, and to photograph staff only with their consent. Photos without flash are generally fine in the permanent galleries. Temporary exhibitions can differ, so check the sign at each room's entrance.
card.challenge: Take the same castle shot three times, shuffling a few steps left or right each time, and see which one puts the towers in the cosiest spot behind the trees.
card.good_to_know: Gustav Gull built the museum in 1898 in the historicist style, modelled on French Renaissance city chateaux. It has dozens of towers, courtyards and a park, on the peninsula between the rivers Sihl and Limmat. It was expanded between 2013 and 2016, but the old castle silhouette is still the star.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head into Platzspitz park and stand on the park lawns or along the Platzpromenade. Face the museum across the water. If you're coming from Zürich HB, the museum lies to the south-east, about 2 minutes on foot.

card.hook: You're on a bridge with the river sliding underneath, the Fraumünster's spire ahead of you and the Grossmünster behind you. That's two postcards from one spot, so don't leave after the first.
card.stand_here: Stand on Münsterbrücke, in the middle of the bridge, and face west towards the Fraumünster. The spire and the Limmat fit in one frame, and the Grossmünster is behind you when you turn around.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the spire, the river and the edge of the bridge in one shot. Then try 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the spire and clock detail. Save zoom 0.5x for Münsterhof, where you're close to the facade.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the spire up with a vertical line so the tower stands straight, with a bit of river along the bottom to lead the eye to the church.
card.best_time: Go at blue hour, when the sky still has colour and the lights are coming on along the river. Switch on night mode and hold your phone still for the few seconds it needs.
card.selfie_here: On Münsterbrücke, step a little aside from the walkway so the Fraumünster is behind you, then use the front camera. For a different backdrop, try Münsterhof square with the church behind you and the baroque buildings around you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Limmatquai promenade, on the east bank across the river, to shoot over the water while you pose with the Fraumünster behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Check that the bridge is open and not blocked by construction before you go. Photos inside the church can be restricted (the Chagall windows especially), so check the signs at the door. Photography stops during services, and flash is not allowed.
card.challenge: Get the spire perfectly straight on a gridline, then spin round and catch the Grossmünster too: two shots, one spot, under a minute.
card.good_to_know: The Fraumünster was built on the remains of an abbey for aristocratic women, founded in 853 by Louis the German for his daughter Hildegard. The abbey was dissolved in 1524 during the Reformation. Inside, five big Chagall windows were installed in 1970, and the organ has 6,959 pipes, the most in the canton.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Münsterbrücke, in the middle of the bridge, and face west towards the Fraumünster. The spire and the Limmat fit in one frame, and the Grossmünster is behind you when you turn around.

card.hook: Picture three stone gents peering down from a white and grey facade: Weber, Wagner and Mozart, with Schiller, Shakespeare and Goethe nearby. The Zurich Opera House is one of the easiest big buildings in town to photograph, because it has a whole plaza to itself.
card.stand_here: Walk onto Sechseläutenplatz and stop on the side facing the opera's front. From there the opera house lies to the south-east, about 1 minute on foot away, so face south-east and take your photos before walking closer.
card.zoom: Start at 1x from further back for a natural look, and switch to 0.5x if you're close and the building won't fit. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the busts and the stone detail above the entrance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the building's vertical edges straight, then tap the facade and drag the brightness slider down a touch so the pale stone keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Late afternoon puts sunlight on the stonework. In the evening the lit building makes a warm, moody picture, so use night mode and keep still while it shoots.
card.selfie_here: Try Sechseläutenplatz, on the square in front of the opera facade near the fountains. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and turn so the building sits over your shoulder. If you'd rather sit down, the public chairs on Bellevue square also have the opera's architecture in view.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone on Sechseläutenplatz and ask them to stand back on the square so they can fit the entire facade in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the facade from the open public plaza. If you want to go inside or take photos indoors, check the official site first. Event stands or public screenings on the plaza can block the view.
card.challenge: Zoom in and catch Weber, Wagner and Mozart in one shot, then see if your friends can name them.
card.good_to_know: The opera company has been based here since 1891. The original theatre was designed by Fellner & Helmer, built in just 16 months after the earlier theatre burnt down, and was the first opera house in Europe with electric lighting. The building was rebuilt in the early 1980s, and the auditorium seats about 1100 people.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk onto Sechseläutenplatz and stop on the side facing the opera's front. From there the opera house lies to the south-east, about 1 minute on foot away, so face south-east and take your photos before walking closer.

card.hook: You step off the tram into a square full of boats, strollers and ringing bells, and then the whole of Lake Zurich opens up in front of you, with the Alps sitting way off at the far end. Nothing gets in the way, so the sky does half the work.
card.stand_here: Walk to the southern edge of Bürkliplatz, onto the Bürkliterrasse, and stand right at the railing. Face south, straight down the lake toward the Alps.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the classic view. Try 0.5x to squeeze in more water and sky, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pull the mountain edge closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the horizon level, then tap the mountains and slide a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Early morning is lovely, when the sky is pale and the water catches the first colours. A clear morning after rain gives the sharpest mountains, and autumn or winter mornings can be very clear too.
card.selfie_here: Take it at the Bürkliterrasse railing on the square's southern edge. Switch to the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it out so the open square sits behind you.
card.challenge: Catch a boat from the landing stage in the foreground with the Alps on the horizon, and keep the water in the bottom third.
card.good_to_know: The square is named after Arnold Bürkli, and the Bürkliterrasse was inaugurated in 1887. It was first topped with two big plaster lions, but the townspeople disliked them and they came down two years later. Today there's a 1952 sculpture by Hermann Hubacher of Zeus as an eagle carrying off Ganymede. The shaded square behind it has a market on Fridays and a flea market on Saturdays, so expect more people then.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the southern edge of Bürkliplatz, onto the Bürkliterrasse, and stand right at the railing. Face south, straight down the lake toward the Alps.

selfie_spots.why: One guide calls this railing the best spot in central Zurich for lake views with the Alps in the distance, and a selfie taken here would have the open square at your back.

card.hook: Most people point their phone straight at Paradeplatz and get a pile of trams and bank walls. The nicer shot is hiding down Bahnhofstrasse, where the trees squeeze the street into a long green tunnel that ends at the lake.
card.stand_here: Stand on Bahnhofstrasse, on the stretch between Paradeplatz and Bürkliplatz, and face towards the lake.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the tree-lined street. Switch to 0.5x when you want the whole square with trams and facades, and try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a tram or a facade detail.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the street in the middle so the trees lead the eye to the lake, and tap the far end of the street so it stays crisp.
card.best_time: Daytime is the best time for the tree-lined view. Give yourself a few minutes, because a tram sliding through the frame adds life to the shot.
card.selfie_here: Try in front of the Sprüngli facade on the square, with the square and its trams behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it so more of the scene fits in, and play with the angle until the facade sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the corner where Bahnhofstrasse meets Paradeplatz and shoot from there, while you stand with the square opening up behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is closed to cars, but it's a busy tram hub. Keep well clear of the tracks and watch for traffic while you line up your picture.
card.challenge: Switch on Live Photo and catch a tram gliding through the frame behind you, without stepping anywhere near the tracks.
card.good_to_know: The UBS building on the west side dates from 1897-1899, the Sprüngli confectioner on the south side opened in 1859, and the hotel at the eastern end opened in 1838. The site was brought inside the town's walls in 1642 and was a livestock market in the 17th century. It got its present name in 1865, after Bahnhofstrasse was built.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Bahnhofstrasse, on the stretch between Paradeplatz and Bürkliplatz, and face towards the lake. Follow the phone icon on the map to find your spot.

card.hook: Here's a small plan: let a tram do the work. Stand by the water as one rolls across the long, low Quaibrücke, with the Fraumünster and St. Peter towers rising behind it, and your photo suddenly has colour and a bit of life.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Utoquai, the lakeside promenade, and look back at the bridge. It lies to the west, so face west. You'll see the Bauschänzli nearby and the two church towers behind the bridge.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole bridge with the towers behind it. Then try 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) to bring the Fraumünster and St. Peter closer. Save zoom 0.5x for when you want lots of promenade and water in the shot.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, sit the bridge on a lower line so it stays level, and leave room above so the towers don't get chopped off.
card.best_time: Go early. The light should fall on the face of the bridge from behind you, and the promenade is likely to be quieter. Around dusk, when the lights come on, night mode works well. Midday is the busiest and the flattest in light.
card.selfie_here: Try the lakeshore path directly below the bridge. Step down from the bridge onto the path underneath it. One guide recommends this lower spot, so use the front camera and see if you can get the bridge over your shoulder. Check the frame when you get there, as no guide confirms the exact angle.
card.rules_and_safety: Trams, cars and cyclists all share the bridge, and traffic can be heavy, so take care if you shoot from it. The bridge also shakes slightly when a tram passes, so wait for a gap between trams. The bridge and the Utoquai are open public road and promenade, so check the official site before you go if works are planned.
card.challenge: Catch a tram crossing the bridge with both church towers still in the frame, and keep the bridge perfectly level on the gridline.
card.good_to_know: The Quaibrücke is the broad bridge where Lake Zurich narrows into the Limmat, linking Bürkliplatz and Bellevueplatz. It dates from the 1880s. The bridge you see today replaced the original in 1984, when the old one was slid aside on steel beams over a single weekend. It got extra width for pedestrians and bikes in 2015.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Utoquai, the lakeside promenade, and look back at the bridge. It lies to the west, so face west. You'll see the Bauschänzli nearby and the two church towers behind the bridge.

card.hook: Most people stand on the Münsterbrücke to photograph the churches, but the bridge looks even better from the riverbank, with cobbles under your feet and old framed houses beside you.
card.stand_here: Stand on Wühre, the cobbled street on the west (left) bank of the Limmat, close to the bridge, and face east across the water to the bridge area and the Grossmünster. Fewer guides mention this spot than the bridge itself, so check it against what you see on the day.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the street, river and bridge in one shot, then try 1x for a more natural view. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) picks out the Grossmünster's towers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the river or the bridge's lower edge on a bottom line, with the church towers rising above it.
card.best_time: Early morning is likely to be quieter on the street and the bridge. Soft light in the morning or evening usually suits the stone and the water.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the middle of the Münsterbrücke, use the front camera, and keep the Grossmünster's twin towers behind you with the Limmat along the bottom of the shot. For a second background, turn to face the opposite bank, where the Fraumünster is the main view.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Wühre, the cobbled street on the west bank close to the bridge, and shoot across the water while you pose on the bridge, then check the photo, because from there they may catch the Grossmünster better than the whole bridge.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge is in the old town's pedestrian zone but still has limited road traffic, so stay on the footpaths and keep your phone steady near the kerb. Trams run on nearby Limmatquai, not across the bridge.
card.challenge: Find the cast-iron railings on the bridge and line them up so they lead your eye straight to the church towers.
card.good_to_know: The Münsterbrücke opened in August 1838 and replaced an older wooden crossing. It has four flat arches and a smaller fifth arch over a former channel, with black Jura marble on the pillars and cast-iron railings. It links the Grossmünster on the east bank with the Fraumünster on the west, and it's listed as a cultural property of national importance.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Wühre, the cobbled street on the west (left) bank of the Limmat, close to the bridge, and face east across the water to the bridge area and the Grossmünster. Fewer guides mention this spot than the bridge itself, so check it against what you see on the day.

card.hook: Most squares show off what's on them. Sechseläutenplatz does the opposite: it's a huge stretch of pale stone, and the empty space is the star.
card.stand_here: Stand on Utoquai, the lakeside stretch opposite the square, at the height of Sechseläutenplatz. Face east towards the square, with the flower boxes along the bottom of your frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole square in. Switch to 0.5x if you want the flower boxes big in the foreground, and try 2x to pick out details on the square.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the flower boxes along the lower third, and keep the phone level so the open square doesn't look tilted.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually means softer light and fewer people. Check the event calendar first, because stalls and tents can fill the square.
card.selfie_here: Head to the fountain at the square, right in front of the Opernhaus, and turn so the Opernhaus is behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x to fit more of the building in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the Bellevue end of the square, facing across it, while you pose out on the square so the Opernhaus fits in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Events can close or block parts of the square, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one super-clean shot: level horizon, flower boxes along the bottom, and nobody in the middle of all that empty space.
card.good_to_know: This is the largest town square in Zurich, and it's named after Sechseläuten, the city's spring festival held here in April. The surface is made of about 110,000 long blocks of Vals quartzite and covers roughly 16,000 square metres. It reopened in early 2014, and digging nearby in 2009 turned up remains of prehistoric pile dwellings.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Utoquai, the lakeside stretch opposite the square, at the height of Sechseläutenplatz. Face east towards the square, with the flower boxes along the bottom of your frame.

card.hook: You hop on a little red funicular at Central, and about a minute and a half later you're standing above the whole Old Town. Not a bad trade for a short ride.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Polyterrasse, at the west end of the balustrade or in the left-hand corner of the terrace, and face out over the Old Town rooftops and church towers. The funicular's line lies to the north-west of this point.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole skyline in, then try 1x for a calmer, more natural look at the rooftops. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) picks out the Grossmünster towers or a patch of Alps.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the distant towers, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Sunset and golden hour are the pick, since the terrace faces west. Go on a clear day if you want the Alps, because summer haze can flatten the mountains, so take a few frames and keep the clearest.
card.selfie_here: Head to the left-hand corner of the Polyterrasse, where the railing doesn't block a wide shot. Use the front camera at 0.5x (if your phone has it) and let the Old Town view sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pavement across the street from the Central tram stop, while you stand in front of the Polybahn lower station entrance at Limmatquai 144.
card.rules_and_safety: If you take photos inside the funicular, be mindful of other passengers and the quick boarding and getting off.
card.challenge: Get the Grossmünster towers dead centre from the western balustrade, with the rooftops filling the lower third and the horizon dead level on the gridlines.
card.good_to_know: The Polybahn opened in 1889 and was first driven by water: a tank under the carriage was filled at the top and emptied at the bottom. It went electric in 1897 and was completely rebuilt in 1996. After a refurbishment closure in spring 2021, it reopened on 17 September 2021.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Polyterrasse, at the west end of the balustrade or in the left-hand corner of the terrace, and face out over the Old Town rooftops and church towers. The funicular's line lies to the north-west of this point.

card.hook: You'll spot the clock before you spot the church. Each face is about 8.7 metres across, among the largest church clock faces in Europe, and it looks very good over the old town rooftops.
card.stand_here: Stand on Lindenhof, at the eastern balustrade edge, and face west. The church is about 1 minute on foot, to the west, so the tower and clock face sit right above the old town in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole scene. Then try 2x to 5x to pick out the tower and clock face (higher zooms depend on your phone). Save zoom 0.5x for St. Peterhofstatt, when you're looking up at the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and keep the tower upright along one of the vertical lines, with a bit of rooftop at the bottom.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or at sunset, when the light is softer and the square is quieter.
card.selfie_here: Try the quiet Schlüsselgasse alley beside the church, where the tower rises overhead. Hold the front camera low, use 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the tower tower over your shoulder (check the framing on the spot). The Lindenhof terrace, the hilltop square above the Limmat, is another good backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone on the Limmatquai, across the river from St. Peter, to take your photo with the river in the foreground and the tower filling the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine for private use, but skip the flash, and don't take any during services. The church or tower may have scaffolding or be closed for work, so check before you go.
card.challenge: From St. Peterhofstatt, hold your phone low and shoot upwards. Can you fit the giant clock face and a few treetops in the same frame?
card.good_to_know: The tower is 64 metres tall, and its pointed wooden roof is the only wooden one in the city. It was re-covered with larch shingles in 1996. A church has stood on this site since the 8th or 9th century, and the present building was consecrated in 1706.

card.hook: Most town halls keep their feet dry. Zurich's Rathaus has its walls rising straight out of the Limmat, so one photo gets you the building, the river and the old-town bank.
card.stand_here: Stand on Rathausbrücke, about 23 m to the north-west of the Town Hall, so the Town Hall sits to the south-east of you. Face south-east and you'll see its riverside facade across the water.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole facade and the river. Then try zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the walls and windows.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, keep the building's vertical lines straight, and put the water in the bottom third so the Town Hall seems to rise out of the river.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the light feels soft and even, and have a look at the facade when you arrive. A renovation is planned, so scaffolding or covers may be in the way.
card.selfie_here: Rathausbrücke itself is a good selfie spot, right next to the Rathaus at the river's east end. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x and tilt the phone until the Town Hall shows over your shoulder. Check the framing on the spot to see which way works best.
card.ask_someone: Walk over to Münsterbrücke, where the Town Hall's south face stands over the water, and ask a passer-by to take your picture with the building in the background.
card.rules_and_safety: Only the outside of the Town Hall can be photographed, because the interior isn't open to visitors. If the facade is covered for renovation, try Münsterbrücke or Wühre instead.
card.challenge: Get the Town Hall and its reflection-lit riverbank in one shot, with the water in the bottom third, and no scaffolding in sight if you can.
card.good_to_know: The Rathaus was built between 1694 and 1698, replacing an earlier town hall from 1397. It was the seat of government of the Republic of Zurich until 1798. The canton of Zurich has owned it since 1803, and today it houses both the cantonal parliament and the City Parliament.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Rathausbrücke, about 23 m to the north-west of the Town Hall, so the Town Hall sits to the south-east of you. Face south-east and you'll see its riverside facade across the water.

card.hook: Picture a church perched on its own little island, with a river on both sides and the Grossmünster towers peeking over its shoulder. That's the Wasserkirche, and it's one of the easiest Old Town scenes to fit into one photo.
card.stand_here: Head to Münsterhof and stand on the Stadthausquai side, facing the river. The Wasserkirche is to the east, about 3 minutes on foot. Look east across the Limmat and you'll see the church straight ahead, with the Helmhaus on its left.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the church, the Helmhaus and the Grossmünster behind them. Then try 2x or more for a tighter shot of the church and towers (higher zooms depend on your phone). Use 0.5x only if you want lots of river and sky.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the river along the lower third with the church just off-centre, and keep your phone level so the walls stay upright.
card.best_time: Afternoon and early evening are likely to be kind, because the sun should be behind you and light up the front of the church. Early morning can be quiet and pleasant, but the sun will be behind the church, so expect a brighter sky.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the Ulrich Zwingli monument on the Limmatquai side, in front of the church's choir, so the Wasserkirche should be right behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a bit above eye level, and tap 0.5x if your phone offers it to fit more church over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: On the Quaibrücke, hand your phone to a passer-by and pose with the Limmat and the churches behind you. The Wasserkirche and Grossmünster both show in that view.
card.rules_and_safety: The viewpoint is an open public square. If you want to go inside the church or the Helmhaus, check the official site first, as exhibitions and services may restrict photos.
card.challenge: Take three frames of the church with different amounts of river in front, then pick your favourite and see if you chose the one with the most water.
card.good_to_know: The Wasserkirche ("water church") is first mentioned around 1250, and its rebuild was finished in 1486. After the Reformation it became Zurich's first public library, in 1634. The island was joined to the right bank in 1839 when the Limmatquai was built.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Münsterhof and stand on the Stadthausquai side, facing the river. The Wasserkirche is to the east, about 3 minutes on foot. Look east across the Limmat and you'll see the church straight ahead, with the Helmhaus on its left.

card.hook: Picture a neat, colourful row of narrow old houses lined up right on the water, like they're still waiting for the boats to land. That's the Schipfe, and the best view of it is from across the river.
card.stand_here: Stand on Limmatquai, on the east bank of the Limmat near the Rathausbrücke end. Face west across the river to the Schipfe houses, with the Rathausbrücke at the left edge of your frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole row of houses in. Try 0.5x if you want more water and sky, but check the houses at the edges don't look stretched. Use 2x to pick out a few facades or windows.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line a horizontal one up with the water's edge, so the houses sit straight and the rooflines don't lean.
card.best_time: An evenly overcast day works nicely for this view. If you're shooting into a bright sky, tap the houses and drag the slider to darker so the facades keep their colour.
card.selfie_here: Head to the landing stage by the water at Schipfe 10 (the Limmatclub). Use the front camera, face the river and let the old Schipfe houses fill the background behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on Limmatquai, across the water, to shoot over the river while you stand on the Schipfe side with the houses behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The landing stage belongs to the Limmatclub, so check it's open to the public before you step on. Also check on site for any closures or building work along the riverfront.
card.challenge: Get the whole row in one shot with the water's edge dead level on the grid, and no passers-by wandering through. Patience wins this one.
card.good_to_know: The name goes back to 1292, when it was written "Schüpfi", meaning a place where boats land. Historians also suggest this was part of the civilian harbour of Roman Turicum. Today it's mostly homes, with a few small shops that are easy to miss.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Limmatquai, on the east bank of the Limmat near the Rathausbrücke end. Face west across the river to the Schipfe houses, with the Rathausbrücke at the left edge of your frame.

card.hook: Turn your back on the grand building for a second and you'll see why people hang around here: old town roofs, the Uetliberg hill, and on clear days the Alps. Then turn back, because the big neoclassical facade is the star, and the terrace gives you room to fit it all in.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Polyterrasse, in the left-hand corner of the terrace, where the railing stays out of your frame. Face east and the main building is straight ahead of you, across the terrace.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole facade and some terrace in one go. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the cupola or the roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines, line the facade up with the horizontal lines and hold the phone level at chest height so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Sunset, according to several guides, because the terrace faces west. On a clear evening the low light may suit both the facade and the view out over the city.
card.selfie_here: Use the same left-hand corner of the Polyterrasse, where the railing is out of the frame. Switch to the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and keep the main building over your shoulder. If you'd like an indoor one, the main hall staircase under the glass roof works by day, but check opening times first.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand out on the Polyterrasse, facing the facade, and frame you with the building behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The main building's forecourt is under renovation, which may affect photos there. The terrace and public areas are reported to be open without booking, but hours vary, so check the official site. A viewpoint guide says the Polyterrasse stays calm and safe even into the evening.
card.challenge: Take one frame where the facade's vertical lines are dead straight, then turn around and see if you can spot the Uetliberg hill.
card.good_to_know: The main building was built between 1858 and 1864 to designs by Gottfried Semper, and the cupola was added in the early 1900s. ETH was founded in 1854, and locals still call it 'Poly' after its old name as a federal polytechnic school. Albert Einstein is one of its best-known associates.
